title: Transmission-Based Precautions

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish contact, droplet, and airborne precautions and the transmission route each targets.
- Explain when each type of transmission-based precaution is used, using common disease examples.
- Select the correct personal protective equipment (PPE) for each precaution type and for standard precautions.
- Apply correct donning, doffing, hand hygiene, and patient-transport practices for isolation.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Standard precautions are like buckling your seatbelt every time you get in the car: you do it for every single ride, even if nothing seems wrong, because you never know what might happen.

### Question 2

Standard precautions are the everyday rules for everyone; transmission-based precautions are like adding an umbrella on top when it is raining. You keep your normal clothes on and add the extra layer.

### Question 3

Your hands are like buses that germs ride on to travel from one person to another. Washing them at the right times stops the bus before any germs get off.

### Question 4

Contact precautions are like wearing an apron and gloves to wash messy dishes: you cover your hands and clothes so nothing yucky touches your skin.

### Question 5

A surgical mask is like holding up a shield in front of your nose and mouth so the big spit droplets from a cough or sneeze bounce off and do not reach you.

### Question 6

An N95 respirator is like a super-tight superhero mask that seals around your nose and mouth so even the tiniest floating germs cannot sneak in around the edges.

### Question 7

Contact spread is like sharing a pencil: the germs hop from one person to the pencil and then to the next person who touches it.

### Question 8

Droplets are like heavy raindrops from a sneeze: they are big and heavy, so they fall down close by instead of floating across the whole room.

### Question 9

Airborne germs are like dust motes or smoke: tiny and floaty, so they can drift through the air and across the room for a long time.

### Question 10

C. diff germs hide on surfaces and hands like sticky glitter. You wear gloves and a gown and wash carefully with soap and water so the glitter does not spread to the next person.

### Question 11

MRSA is a tough germ that rides on hands and surfaces. Gloves and a gown stop it from hitching a ride to the next patient.

### Question 12

Flu germs fly out in big sneeze and cough drops. A surgical mask catches those drops before they reach your nose and mouth.

### Question 13

Whooping cough germs shoot out in cough drops. A mask stops those drops, like catching a water balloon before it bursts on you.

### Question 14

TB germs are like invisible dust that floats in the air for a long time. You need a sealed room and a tight special mask so you do not breathe them in.

### Question 15

Measles germs are like super-floaty glitter that hangs in the air long after the person leaves the room. You need a tight mask and special airflow to stay safe.

### Question 16

A surgical mask is like a loose curtain, while an N95 is like a fitted diving mask that seals tight so no air leaks in around the edges.

### Question 17

Gloves are like a raincoat for your hands: any time you might touch something wet or yucky like blood, you put them on first.

### Question 18

A gown is like a big splash apron you wear when cooking something that might spatter, so your clothes stay clean and safe.

### Question 19

Goggles are like safety glasses in shop class: you wear them when there is a chance something could splash toward your eyes.

### Question 20

Bloodborne germs are the ones that travel in blood. The big three to remember are hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV.

### Question 21

Gloves are like disposable sandwich bags: they can have tiny holes, so after you take them off you wash your hands to be sure nothing got through.

### Question 22

Meningitis germs ride on cough and sneeze drops, so a mask stops them, just like catching raindrops with an umbrella.

### Question 23

Scabies is caused by tiny bugs that crawl from one person's skin to another, so gloves and a gown stop them from hitching a ride.

### Question 24

Chickenpox germs can float through the air like smoke and also hide in the spots on the skin, so you need both a tight mask and gloves and a gown.

### Question 25

Rubella germs travel in sneeze and cough drops, so a mask catches them before they reach your nose and mouth.

### Question 26

Mumps germs spread through spit and sneeze drops, so a mask blocks them just like a goalie blocks a shot.

### Question 27

Strep throat germs fly out on sneeze drops, so a mask catches them like a net catches falling leaves.

### Question 28

RSV spreads two ways, like a germ that both sneezes and sticks to surfaces, so you need a mask plus gloves and a gown to block both paths.

### Question 29

Impetigo has weepy spots that ooze germs, so gloves and a gown keep those germs off your skin and clothes.

### Question 30

VRE is a super-tough germ that rides on hands and surfaces, so gloves and a gown keep it from traveling to someone else.

### Question 31

C. diff makes tiny armor-covered seeds called spores. Alcohol cannot break the armor, but soap and water scrub the seeds right off your hands.

### Question 32

Norovirus is a super-contagious tummy bug. Wash with soap and water and use gloves and a gown so the bug does not jump to the next person.

### Question 33

Equipment is like a shared toy: after one sick friend plays with it, you either keep it only for them or wash it well before the next friend touches it.

### Question 34

Take off the dirty apron and gloves right at the door, like taking off muddy boots before coming inside, then wash your hands.

### Question 35

When a sick patient walks through the halls, you cover their ouchy spots and warn the next room, like keeping a leaky paint can sealed and telling the next room it is coming.

### Question 36

The patient wears a mask while walking through the halls, like covering your mouth when you cough, so their germs stay with them.

### Question 37

An airborne patient wears a mask and takes the shortest, emptiest path, like carrying a smoky candle through the house carefully so the smoke does not spread.

### Question 38

Droplets are like heavy spitballs: they only fly a few feet before falling, so you need a mask when you are close to the thrower.

### Question 39

When you are up close and something might splash toward your eyes, you add goggles on top of your mask, like wearing both a hat and an umbrella in a storm.

### Question 40

If someone is coughing in the waiting room, hand them a tissue-and-mask and give them a quieter spot, like moving a sneezing friend away from the snack table.

### Question 41

If someone might have TB, treat them like they do until proven otherwise: a special room that keeps their air from drifting into the hallway.

### Question 42

A negative-pressure room is like a vacuum: air is always being sucked inward, so any floating germs get pulled in instead of leaking out under the door.

### Question 43

The door is like the lid on a smoky pot: keep it closed so the smoke stays inside instead of filling the kitchen.

### Question 44

An N95 only works if it hugs your face just right, so you get a special check to make sure it fits your face like a glove.

### Question 45

Every time you put on the tight mask, you give it a quick puff-and-squeeze test to make sure no air is leaking around the edges, like checking a bicycle tire for leaks.

### Question 46

A gown is like a big backward apron that covers your front and arms and ties shut, so nothing yucky can touch your clothes or skin.

### Question 47

You peel off the dirtiest things first — gloves, then goggles, then the apron, and the mask comes off last — like undressing after a muddy game so the mud stays on the outside.

### Question 48

You suit up in order: apron first, then mask, then goggles, and gloves go on very last so they seal over the sleeves.

### Question 49

The sign on the door is like the rules posted before a roller coaster: it tells everyone exactly what gear and steps they need before they can go in.

### Question 50

Cohorting is like putting all the kids with the same cold in one playroom: they cannot give each other the cold they already have.

### Question 51

If the shingles spots are covered up like a bandaged knee, the germs stay put, so normal careful rules are enough.

### Question 52

When shingles spreads all over the body, its germs can float in the air and hide on the skin, so you need both the tight mask and the gloves and gown.

### Question 53

Chickenpox is a two-way germ: it floats in the air and also hides in the blister fluid, so you block both the air path and the touch path.

### Question 54

The cuff is like a shared bicycle helmet: after one person uses it with sweaty, germy skin, you clean it before the next person puts it on.

### Question 55

Sharps go in the special hard box, like putting broken glass in a thick container so no one gets poked when they take out the trash.

### Question 56

Never put the cap back on a needle with two hands, because your fingers can get poked. Use a safety device or a one-handed trick instead.

### Question 57

If you get poked, wash it with soap and water right away and tell a grown-up in charge immediately, like telling the teacher right after you get a cut at school.

### Question 58

Take off the dirty gear right at the edge of the work area, like taking off muddy shoes at the front door instead of tracking mud through the house.

### Question 59

Soap and water is for when your hands are actually dirty or after a spore-y germ like C. diff; the quick gel is for when they look clean.

### Question 60

A patient whose body's germ-fighters are weak is like a plant in a fragile pot: keep them away from sick people and dusty construction so they stay safe.

### Question 61

Pneumonia germs ride on cough drops, so a mask catches them the way a catcher's mitt catches a ball.

### Question 62

If a wound keeps leaking through the bandage, germs can get on everything it touches, so gloves and a gown are needed.

### Question 63

Lice crawl from one head to another, so gloves and a gown and not sharing hats or brushes keep them from moving to the next person.

### Question 64

Big droplets drop like pebbles, so a regular mask and some distance catch them. Tiny airborne germs float like dust, so you need the extra-tight mask.

### Question 65

If the right safety gear is missing, you do not go in without it — you go get the gear and tell someone it needs restocking, like grabbing a helmet before riding a bike.

### Question 66

If someone might have a super-catchy illness, act fast: mask them, give them their own space away from others, and tell the nurse right away.

### Question 67

Chickenpox is sneaky because it spreads both through the air and through the blister spots, so you need the tight mask plus gloves and a gown.

### Question 68

Taking down the caution sign is the doctor's or safety team's job, not something you decide just because the patient looks better.

### Question 69

Airborne germs are like microscopic dust, so tiny they can float in the air for a long time and ride on air currents across a room.

### Question 70

If the tight mask cannot seal because of a beard, a powered hood with its own air supply can protect the person instead, like wearing a space helmet.

### Question 71

If your face changes — like growing a beard or losing weight — the mask might not hug your face anymore, so you get re-checked to be sure it still seals.

### Question 72

When a germ spreads two ways, you wear two sets of gear at once: gloves and apron for the touch path, plus a mask for the sneeze path.

### Question 73

Match the germ to its travel route: TB floats in the air (airborne), flu rides on sneezes (droplet), and C. diff sticks to hands and surfaces (contact).

### Question 74

Airborne plus contact is the full suit: tight mask for the air, and gloves and apron for the touch path, all worn together.

### Question 75

COVID spreads on sneeze drops and by touch, so you wear a mask, gloves, and eye protection; only for special mist-making procedures do you need the extra-tight mask.

### Question 76

Some procedures create a mist of tiny germs, so the person doing them needs the super-tight mask, like wearing a full face shield when using a power saw.

### Question 77

C. diff leaves behind tough little armor-coated seeds on surfaces that can survive for a long time, so the room needs a really good scrub.

### Question 78

If someone's symptoms look like TB, treat it like an emergency: mask them, give them their own room, and get the nurse right away so their air does not mix with everyone else's.

### Question 79

If you are not protected and you are around measles, tell the boss right away and follow the safety plan, because you might need to stay home so you do not pass it on.

### Question 80

Measles is the floaty-air germ in this list; the others ride on big sneeze drops that fall quickly.

### Question 81

When you do not yet know what the cough is, play it safe: give the patient a mask and use careful habits, and if it could be TB, use the special air room.

### Question 82

Throwaway items are like a used napkin: use it once for that person and toss it, rather than passing it to the next person.

### Question 83

Only the safety plan and the health experts decide if a tight mask can be used again; it is not a choice you make on your own.

### Question 84

Scabies is a touch-only germ, but chickenpox is a touch-plus-air germ, so chickenpox needs the bigger, tighter protection.

### Question 85

You keep the mask rules going until the medicine has worked for the right amount of time, not just until the person's fever dips.

### Question 86

The special room's air is like dirty water that must be piped outside or run through a super-filter before it can go back into the building.

### Question 87

Wash at five special times: before touching a patient, before a clean task, after touching anything wet or yucky, after touching the patient, and after touching their stuff.

### Question 88

If someone who is pregnant might have been around chickenpox, tell the nurse right away so they can get the right help, because chickenpox can be extra dangerous during pregnancy.

### Question 89

Super-germs are hard to beat with medicine, so the best plan is to stop them from spreading in the first place with gloves, gowns, and cleaning.

### Question 90

If someone has runny tummy trouble right after antibiotics, treat it as the spore-y germ until proven otherwise: gloves, gown, soap and water, and tell the nurse.
